# Computer Science > Machine Learning **arXiv:2602.03211** (cs) \[Submitted on 3 Feb 2026\] # Title:Lookahead Sample Reward Guidance for Test-Time Scaling of Diffusion Models Authors: [Yeongmin Kim](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Kim,+Y), [Donghyeok Shin](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Shin,+D), [Byeonghu Na](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Na,+B), [Minsang Park](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Park,+M), [Richard Lee Kim](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Kim,+R+L), [Il-Chul Moon](https://arxiv.org/search/cs?searchtype=author&query=Moon,+I) View a PDF of the paper titled Lookahead Sample Reward Guidance for Test-Time Scaling of Diffusion Models, by Yeongmin Kim and 5 other authors [View PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.03211) [HTML (experimental)](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.03211v1) > Abstract:Diffusion models have demonstrated strong generative performance; however, generated samples often fail to fully align with human intent. This paper studies a test-time scaling method that enables sampling from regions with higher human-aligned reward values. Existing gradient guidance methods approximate the expected future reward (EFR) at an intermediate particle \\mathbf{x}\_t using a Taylor approximation, but this approximation at each time step incurs high computational cost due to sequential neural backpropagation. We show that the EFR at any \\mathbf{x}\_t can be computed using only marginal samples from a pre-trained diffusion model. The proposed EFR formulation detaches the neural dependency between \\mathbf{x}\_t and the EFR, enabling closed-form guidance computation without neural backpropagation. To further improve efficiency, we introduce lookahead sampling to collect marginal samples. For final sample generation, we use an accurate solver that guides particles toward high-reward lookahead samples. We refer to this sampling scheme as LiDAR sampling. LiDAR achieves substantial performance improvements using only three samples with a 3-step lookahead solver, exhibiting steep performance gains as lookahead accuracy and sample count increase; notably, it reaches the same GenEval performance as the latest gradient guidance method for SDXL with a 9.5x speedup. | | | | --- | --- | | Comments: | Under Review | | Subjects: | Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) | | Cite as: | [arXiv:2602.03211](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03211) \[cs.LG\] | | | (or [arXiv:2602.03211v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03211v1) \[cs.LG\] for this version) | | | [https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2602.03211](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2602.03211)

## Abstract

### Abstract

Time-series forecasting has been actively studied and adopted in various real-world domains. Recently there have been two research mainstreams in this area: building Transformer-based architectures such as Informer, Autoformer and Reformer, and developing time-series representation learning frameworks based on contrastive learning such as TS2Vec and CoST. Both efforts have greatly improved the performance of time series forecasting. In this paper, we investigate a novel direction towards improving the forecasting performance even more, which is orthogonal to the aforementioned mainstreams as a model-agnostic scheme. We focus on time stamp embeddings that has been less-focused in the literature. Our idea is simple-yet-effective: based on given current time stamp, we predict embeddings of its near future time stamp and utilize the predicted embeddings in the time-series (value) forecasting task. We believe that if such future time information can be previewed at the time of prediction, they can be utilized by any time-series forecasting models as useful additional information. Our experimental results confirmed that our method consistently and significantly improves the accuracy of the recent Transformer-based models and time-series representation learning frameworks. Our code is available at: https://github.com/sunsunmin/Look\_Ahead

Learning with Lookahead:
Can History-Based Models Rival Globally Optimized Models?

Yoshimasa Tsuruoka $ ^{\\dagger \*} $

Yusuke Miyao $ ^{ \\ddagger \*} $

Jun'ichi Kazama $ ^{\*} $

$ ^{\\dagger} $ Japan Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (JAIST), Japan

$ ^{\\ddagger} $ National Institute of Informatics (NII), Japan

- National Institute of Information and Communications Technology (NICT), Japan [tsuruoka@jaist.ac.jp](mailto:tsuruoka@jaist.ac.jp) [yusuke@nii.ac.jp](mailto:yusuke@nii.ac.jp) [kazama@nict.go.jp](mailto:kazama@nict.go.jp)

Abstract

This paper shows that the performance of history-based models can be significantly improved by performing lookahead in the state space when making each classification decision. Instead of simply using the best action output by the classifier, we determine the best action by looking into possible sequences of future actions and evaluating the final states realized by those action sequences. We present a perceptron-based parameter optimization method for this learning framework and show its convergence properties. The proposed framework is evaluated on partof-speech tagging, chunking, named entity recognition and dependency parsing, using standard data sets and features. Experimental results demonstrate that history-based models with lookahead are as competitive as globally optimized models including conditional random fields (CRFs) and structured perceptrons.

1 Introduction

Although history-based models have many practical merits, their accuracy is often surpassed by globally optimized models such as CRFs (Lafferty et al., 2001) and structured perceptrons (Collins, 2002), mainly due to the label bias problem. Today, vanilla history-based models such as maximum entropy Markov models (MEMMs) are probably not the first choice for those who are looking for a machine learning model that can deliver the state-of-the-art accuracy for their NLP task. Globally optimized models, by contrast, are gaining popularity in the community despite their relatively high computational cost.

In this paper, we argue that history-based models are not something that should be left behind in research history, by demonstrating that their accuracy can be significantly improved by incorporating a lookahead mechanism into their decisionmaking process. It should be emphasized that we use the word "lookahead" differently from some literature on syntactic parsing in which lookahead simply means looking at the succeeding words to choose the right parsing actions. In this paper, we use the word to refer to the process of choosing the best action by considering different sequences of future actions and evaluating the structures realized by those sequences. In other words, we introduce a lookahead mechanism that performs a search in the space of future actions.

2 Motivation

To answer the question of whether the historybased models enhanced with lookahead can actually compete with globally optimized models, we evaluate the proposed framework with a range of standard NLP tasks, namely, POS tagging, text chunking (a.k.a. shallow parsing), named entity recognition, and dependency parsing.

This paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the idea of lookahead with a motivating example from dependency parsing. Section 3 describes our search algorithm for lookahead and a perceptron-based training algorithm. Experimental results on POS tagging, chunking, named entity recognition, and dependency parsing are presented in Section 4. We discuss relationships between our approach and some related work in Section 5. Section 6 offers concluding remarks with some potential research directions.

This section describes an example of dependency parsing that motivates the introduction of lookahead in history-based models.

In the lookahead strategy, we make this decision by referring to future states. For example, if we apply shift to State 4, we will reach State 8 in the end which indicates that "with" attaches to "dog". The other way, i.e., applying reduce $ R $ to State 4, eventually arrives at State 9', indicating "with" attaches to "saw". These future states indicate that we were implicitly resolving PP-attachment ambiguity at State 4. While conventional methods attempt to resolve such ambiguity using surrounding features at State 4, the lookahead approach resolves the same ambiguity by referring to the future states, for example, State 8 and 9'. Because future states can provide additional and valuable information for ambiguity resolution, improved accuracy is expected.

This section presents four sets of experimental results to show how the lookahead process improves the accuracy of history-based models in common NLP tasks.

The first set of experiments is about POS tagging. The training and test data were created from the Wall Street Journal corpus of the Penn Treebank (Marcus et al., 1994). Sections 0-18 were used as the training data. Sections 19-21 were used for tuning the meta parameters for learning (the number of iterations and the margin C). Sections 22-24 were used for the final accuracy reports.

The experimental results are shown in Table 1. Note that the models in the top four rows use exactly the same feature set. It is clearly seen that the lookahead improves tagging accuracy, and our historybased models with lookahead is as accurate as the CRF model. We also created another set of models by simply adding tag trigram features, which cannot be employed by first-order CRF models. These features have slightly improved the tagging accuracy, and the final accuracy achieved by a search depth of 3 was comparable to some of the best results achieved by pure supervised learning in this task (Shen et al., 2007; Lavergne et al., 2010).

The second set of experiments is about chunking. We used the data set for the CoNLL 2000 shared task, which contains 8,936 sentences where each token is annotated with the "IOB" tags representing text chunks. The experimental results are shown in Table 2. Again, our history-based models with lookahead were slightly more accurate than the CRF model using exactly the same set of features. The accuracy achieved by the lookahead model with a search depth of 2 was comparable to the accuracy achieved by a computationally heavy combination of max-margin classifiers (Kudo and Matsumoto, 2001). We also tested the effectiveness of additional features of tag trigrams using the development data, but there was no improvement in the accuracy.

Table 3 shows the experimental results, together with some previous performance reports achieved by pure machine leaning methods (i.e. without rulebased post processing or external resources such as gazetteers). Our history-based model with no lookahead was considerably worse than the CRF model using the same set of features, but it was significantly improved by the introduction of lookahead and resulted in accuracy figures better than that of the CRF model.

4.2 Dependency parsing

We also evaluate our method in dependency parsing. We follow the most standard experimental setting for English dependency parsing: The Wall Street Journal portion of Penn Treebank is converted to dependency trees by using the head rules of Yamada and Matsumoto (2003). $ ^{3} $ The data is split into training (section 02-21), development (section 22), and test (section 23) sets. The parsing accuracy was evaluated with auto-POS data, i.e., we used our lookahead POS tagger (depth = 2) presented in the previous subsection to assign the POS tags for the development and test data. Unlabeled attachment scores for all words excluding punctuations are reported. The development set is used for tuning the meta parameters, while the test set is used for evaluating the final accuracy.

The parsing algorithm is the "arc-standard" method (Nivre, 2004), which is briefly described in Section 2. With this algorithm, state $ S $ corresponds to a parser configuration, i.e., the stack and the queue, and action $ a $ corresponds to shift, reduce $ L $ and reduce $ R $ . The table also lists accuracy figures reported in the literature on shift-reduce dependency parsing. Most of the latest studies on shift-reduce dependency parsing employ dynamic programing or beam search, which implies that deterministic methods were not as competitive as those methods. It should also be noted that all of the listed studies learn structured perceptrons (Collins and Roark, 2004), while our parser learns locally optimized perceptrons. In this table, our parser without lookahead search (i.e. depth = 0) resulted in significantly lower accuracy than the previous studies. In fact, it is worse than the deterministic parser of Huang et al. (2009), which uses (almost) the same set of features. This is presumably due to the difference between locally optimized perceptrons and globally optimized structured perceptrons. However, our parser with lookahead search is significantly better than their deterministic parser, and its accuracy is close to the levels of the parsers with beam search.

5 Discussion

The reason why we introduced a lookahead mechanism into history-based models is that we wanted the model to be able to avoid making such mistakes that can be detected only in later stages. Probabilistic history-based models such as MEMMs should be able to avoid (at least some of) such mistakes by performing a Viterbi search to find the highest probability path of the actions. However, as pointed out by Lafferty et al. (2001), the per-state normalization of probabilities makes it difficult to give enough penalty to such incorrect sequences of actions, and that is primarily why MEMMs are outperformed by CRFs.

\| 14\. ABSTRACT
While significant strides had been made in deep learning in the 5 years subsequent to its resurgence (2012), a large part of this success was through large-scale training of deep neural networks on labeled data. Transfer learning was commonly used, but in reality understanding how to effectively fine-tune pre-trained models (such as those pre-trained on ImageNet \[8\]) was not well understood. For example, the methods were susceptible to a shift in the data distribution from the source dataset (domain shift) and it was often not clear where to transfer from given a new problem. While early methods involving unsupervised, semi-supervised, domain adaptation, and few-shot learning had been developed (including by this team), they lacked small subsets of real-world problems and in practice often could not beat strong baselines with transfer learning alone \[9\]. Since then, the landscape has drastically changed, and the methods developed under this program as well as by the community at large have enabled the usage of large-scale unlabelled pre-training combined with semi-supervised learning to significantly increase performance under low-labeled conditions. Their team contributed a significant number of advancements to this body of work, ranging from scientific formulations and understanding of the problems to the development of practical algorithms that performed well under both established academic datasets to the evaluations. Their work viewed these low-labelled problems by explicitly representing the structure of the data manifold using graph representations. Through this lens, they proposed a number of innovations that answer the question of how to improve their transfer and wires to transfer from them. # 1.0 Summary

While significant strides had been made in deep learning in the 5 years subsequent to its resurgence (2012), a large part of this success was through large-scale training of deep neural networks on labeled data. Transfer learning was commonly used, but in reality understanding how to effectively fine-tune pre- trained models (such as those pre-trained on ImageNet \[8\]) was not well understood. For example, the methods were susceptible to a shift in the data distribution from the source dataset (domain shift) and it was often not clear where to transfer from given a new problem. While early methods involving unsupervised, semi-supervised, domain adaptation, and few-shot learning had been developed (including by this team), they tackled small subsets of real-world problems and in practice often could not beat strong baselines with transfer learning alone \[9\]. Since then, the landscape has drastically changed, and the methods developed under this program as well as by the community at large have enabled the usage of large-scale unlabeled pre-training combined with semi-supervised learning to significantly increase performance under low-labeled conditions. Our team contributed a significant number of advancements to this body of work, ranging from scientific formulations and understanding of the problems to the development of practical algorithms that performed well under both established academic datasets to the evaluations. Our work viewed these low-labeled problems by explicitly representing the structure of the data _manifold using graph representations. Through this lens, we proposed a number of innovations that_ answer the questions of what to transfer, how to transfer, and where to transfer from. We have specifically developed methods for 1) Leveraging the Manifold-Structure through FeatMatch \[13\], 2) Leveraging the Manifold-Structure through Manifold Transport Operators \[14, 15, 16, 17, 18\], 3) **Semi-Supervised Clustering and Retrieval for Zero-Shot Learning \[19\], 4) Low-Labeled Captioning** **through Retrieval \[20, 21\], 5) Semi-Supervised Object Detection through Cross-Match , and 6)** **Advancements in Active Learning.** Our methods have been published at top venues including: CVPR, ECCV, NeurIPS ICML, AAAI, UAI, and TMLR. # 2.0 Introduction

While significant strides had been made in deep learning in the 5 years subsequent to its resurgence (2012), a large part of this success was through large-scale training of deep neural networks on labeled data. Transfer learning was commonly used, but in reality understanding how to effectively fine-tune pre- trained models (such as those pre-trained on ImageNet\[8\]) was not well-understood. For example, the methods were susceptible to a shift in the data distribution from the source dataset (domain shift) and it was often not clear where to transfer from given a new problem. While early methods involving unsupervised, semi-supervised, domain adaptation, and few-shot learning had been developed (including by this team), they tackled small subsets of real-world problems and in practice often could not beat strong baselines with transfer learning alone \[9\]. Since then, the landscape has drastically changed, and the methods developed under this program as well as by the community at large have enabled the usage of large-scale unlabeled pre-training combined with semi-supervised learning to significantly increase performance under low-labeled conditions. Our team contributed a significant number of advancements to this body of work, ranging from scientific formulations and understanding of the problems to the development of practical algorithms that performed well under both established academic datasets to the evaluations. Our work viewed these low-labeled problems by explicitly representing the structure of the data _manifold using graph representations. Through this lens, we proposed a number of innovations that_ answer the questions of what to transfer, how to transfer, and where to transfer from. The basis of _what to transfer is formed by our previous work \[10, 11\], which shows that similarity comparisons (i.e._ whether two instances are of the same semantic class or not) rather than labels can form the basis of supervised, semi-supervised, cross-task transfer, and domain adaptation within the same framework and achieve state of art results. For example, when a new unlabeled dataset contains completely new categories, we have shown that feature transfer is not as effective as similarity transfer \[10\]. In other words, similarity learning can be transferred across domains, and this can also be augmented via unsupervised learning of similarity (e.g. through weak labels such as those obtained from temporal information), meta-learning, etc. Unlike this previous work, which implicitly optimized classifiers given these constraints, we propose to use these similarity comparisons to explicitly represent the connectivity of instances across a graph, i.e. nodes in the graph (representing instances) are connected via edges weighted by their similarity. Given unlabeled and labeled instances from dissimilar domains (TA 1.1) or similar domains (TA 1.2), we then propose to use graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) \[12\] to propagate feature and label information across the graph to estimate the class labels for new unlabeled instances in a target domain. This forms the basis of how to transfer. As a summary, we highlight a list of our contributions below:

1. **Leveraging the Manifold-Structure through FeatMatch \[13\] - Novel methods for graph** (manifold)-based augmentation for semi-supervised image classification.
2. **Leveraging the Manifold-Structure through Transport Operators \[14, 15, 16, 17, 18\] -** A series of methods for learning manifold transport operators in an efficient manner on real-world data, integrated within semi-supervised learning pipelines to improve performance.
3. \*\*Semi-Supervised Clustering and Retrieval for Zero-Shot Learning \[19\] -\*\*Novel methods for integrating semi- supervised clustering and retrieval, within large-scale pre-trained feature spaces, to perform effective zero-shot learning.
4. \*\*Low-Labeled Captioning through Retrieval \[20, 21\] -\*\*Methods for retrieval-based augmentation of images, which can be seen as additional views of the data, and efficient and effective architectures for exploiting them for low-labeled image captioning.
5. **Semi-Supervised Object Detection through Cross-Match \[22\] - Methods for improving** gradient flow in existing semi-supervised object detection methods to significantly improve performance.

## 3.1 FeatMatch: Manifold Structure for Semi-Supervised Classification

In this section, we present our work on our developed manifold-based augmentation techniques \[13\]. Our focus in the area of semi-supervised classification is two-fold: 1) Advancing results on standard semi-supervised learning datasets and 2) adapting semi-supervised methods and our graph-based feature augmentation to the multi-domain setting. First, we will describe the overall scenario we are setting up. In section 3.1.2 we describe our method and in 4.1 we describe our results that we have obtained for both standard datasets and across data shift.

## 3.1.1 Multi-domain Semi-Supervised Learning

For the LwLL problems, the unlabeled data may come from a domain different from the domain of the target (sparsely) labeled data. For instance, given a small set of labeled natural images of animals, the large unlabeled set may also contain animal images from paintings, sketches, etc. In general, we are interested in the case where there is both semantic shift (i.e. label shift) and non-semantic shift (e.g. different modalities, see Figure 1). Below we describe the setting with only non-semantic shift for which we have preliminary results. We are currently working on investigating either and/or both types of shift. To investigate the effect of domain shift in the unlabeled set, we proposed a new SSL task based on the DomainNet dataset \[24\], which contains 345 classes of images coming from six domains: Clipart, Infograph, Painting, Quickdraw, Real, and Sketch. We use the Real domain as our target. Five percent of the data from the Real domain are kept as the target labeled set, and the rest are the target unlabeled set. We select Painting, Sketch, and Quickdraw as shifted domains. To modulate the level of domain shift in the unlabeled data, we propose a parameter r _u_ that controls the ratio of unlabeled data coming from the target Real domain or the shifted domains. Specifically, r _u_ percent of target Real unlabeled set is replaced with data uniformly drawn from the shifted domains. By formulating the problem this way, the amount of unlabeled data remains constant. The only factor that affects the performance of the proposed method is the ratio between in-domain data and shifted domain data in the unlabeled set. We randomly reserve 1% of data from the Real domain as the validation set. The final result is reported on the test set of the Real domain, with the model selected on the reserved validation set. The images are center-cropped and resized to 128x128 resolution, and the model we use is the standard ResNet-18 \[25\]. There are around 120k training samples, which is more than twice larger than the standard SSL datasets such as CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. For a fair comparison, we fix all hyper- parameters across experiments of different r _u_ to truly assess the robustness of proposed methods toward domain shift in the unlabeled data.

## 3.1.3 Prototype Selection.

In order to efficiently leverage the knowledge of other classes for feature refinement and augmentation, we propose to compactly represent the information of each class by clustering in the feature space. To select representative prototypes from the dataset, we propose to use K-Means clustering in the feature space to extract p _k_ cluster means as prototypes for each class. However, there are two technical challenges: (1) in an SSL setting, most images are unlabeled; (2) even if all the labels are available, it is still computationally expensive to extract features of all the images from the entire dataset before running K-Means. To tackle these issues, as shown in Fig. 4, we collect features _fxi_ and pseudo-labels yˆ _i_ already generated by the network at every iteration of the training loop, i.e., no extra computation needed. In the recording loop, the pairs of pseudo label and features are detached from the computation graph and pushed into a memory bank for later usage. The prototypes are extracted by K-Means at every epoch when we go over the whole dataset. Finally, the feature refinement and augmentation module updates the prototypes with the newly extracted ones in the training loop. Even though the prototypes are extracted from the feature computed from the model a few iterations ago, as training progresses and the model gradually converges, the extracted prototypes fall on the correct cluster and are diverse enough to compactly represent the feature distribution per class. Similar idea is concurrently explored in self- supervised learning by He et al. \[32\].

## 3.3 Semi-Supervised Clustering and Retrieval for Zero-Shot Learning

In this work, we detail our work on zero-shot classification leveraging semi-supervised clustering and retrieval \[19\]. Specifically, we tackle the setting of Novel Category Discovery (NCD) \[53\], which is a problem highly relevant to the LwLL zero-shot evaluation. The problem involves discovering new categories in unlabeled data, by leveraging pre-training or auxiliary training. Recently, Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) \[54\] was formalized to make the setting more realistic, where the goal is to jointly discover unknown categories and classify known categories within the unlabeled data. This setting is related to semi-supervised learning but does not assume we know all of the classes in the data \[55, 56\]. The state-of-the-art methods for this setting utilize self-supervised image pre-training (e.g. DINO \[57\]) as auxiliary information used to encode the images, after which simple clustering is performed \[54\]. However, even though self-supervised feature learning can show some out-of-domain generalization \[58, 59\], it is still a difficult challenge as the features may not be relevant to entirely new categories. Here, we posit that a key missing element to improve such generalization is a more effective encoding of the semantic relationships between object categories. Recently, aligned multi-modal (vision and language) models have shown to give a remarkable boost in generalization of visual learning, especially when scaled up\[60, 61, 62, 63\]. These models are learned via alignment of visual and language embeddings through large-scale contrastive training of paired image-text data \[63\]. Such methods have demonstrated a potential for learning open-world visual concepts, since the textual alignment forces visual features to be nearby similar concepts, and hence new categories can be well- placed in the feature space by the visual encoder. Given the strong zero-shot results of such models, we therefore propose to first replace the uni- modal image encoder with one trained in a multi-modal fashion (CLIP \[63\]). By itself, this simple modification yields significant performance gains, beating all of the current state of art. Hence, this setting can serve as a simple, but extremely strong, baseline. However, in just replacing the visual encoder, we discard the text branch of the multi-modal model and thus fail to fully leverage the joint vision-and-language (VL) embedding and its zero-shot generalizability. Furthermore, despite significant gains, the visual encoder from a multi-modal model can still perform poorly when the visual concepts are not well-represented in their training data and are somewhat out-of-distribution. Here, we propose to augment the visual embeddings with retrieved textual information. This allows us to better leverage the joint VL embedding and the text encoder as well as provide the ability to extend the contextual knowledge available for clustering unknown and potentially out-of-domain categories and images. Specifically, inspired by prior image captioning works \[20\], given an image, we retrieve the top-k most relevant text from a large text corpus \[64, 65\] (which could be from the multi-modal training set itself). We specifically use the alignment between CLIP’s visual encoding (of the image) and textual

## 3.4 Retrieval for Low-Labeled Image Captioning

In this section, we detail our work to support low-labeled image captioning by leveraging both retrieval and effective architectures to fuse the resulting multiple views of data \[20, 21\]. We specifically focus on an important research problem that has remained unanswered: how should we leverage and ensemble _**the information from heterogeneous views?**_ \| \| One naive approach \[73, 74, 75, 76\] is to train \|V\| (number of views) models for each view and average the predictions from these models. Clearly, this method is computationally expensive and completely ignores the difference in the usefulness of each view by ensembling the views with equal weights. Another method \[77, 78, 3\] is to concatenate the views, each represented by a sequence of tokens, into one single long sequence and feed the concatenated sequence to the transformer model \[33\], hoping that the transformer is capable of learning a good strategy to leverage and ensemble the views internally. Although transformer models may have the capacity and flexibility to leverage the information from all views jointly by a transformer encoder, and ensemble the views by learned attention, it has also been shown in the vision transformer community \[79\] that transformer models are notoriously data-hungry. On the popular MS-COCO \[80\] image captioning benchmark with less than 0.6 M training examples, we posit that we should introduce some structural priors to aid the learning of the transformer model \[81, 82\]. To solve this, we leverage a probabilistic interpretation of image captioning models to derive appropriate architectural biases. Specifically, multi-view hierarchical ensembling (illustrated in Fig. 13) emerges naturally in the derivation. Grounded on the derived probability model, at the step of predicting the next word, the model first generates heterogeneous views of the input image by different pre-trained models. These views are then encoded separately. Given the separately encoded views and previously generated words (e.g. “Black bags sitting on top of a” in Fig. 13), the model learns to ensemble the views, putting more attention on views that provide more helpful information for generating the next word. Finally, the next word is generated from the ensembled view. Our proposed strategy is different from previous works in that the views are encoded and ensembeled hierarchically: the model first encodes information within the views, and then ensembles across the encoded views conditioned on previously generated words. Since the views are encoded separately in the proposed multi-view hierarchical ensembling and each view contains partial information of the input image, we also propose to regard each view as an augmentation of the input image. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to propose the idea of generating and regarding heterogeneous multi-modal views, obtained only from the input image, as augmentation in vision and language. The key difference here is that we assume each view contain partial information of the input image, and is treated individually and encoded separately, rather than concatenated and encoded jointly. Data augmentation increases data diversity and has achieved great success in low-label settings such as semi-supervised learning \[28, 51, 13\] and self-supervised learning \[83, 84, 85, 86\]. This is particularly important for training data-hungry transformer models. Furthermore, by regarding each view as an augmentation, we can naturally incorporate contrastive learning to help the representation learning of heterogeneous views. In contrastive learning, given different views (random augmentations) of input images, the views from the same image are pulled together in an embedding space while those from different images are pushed apart. It has been shown \[85, 87, 88\] that contrastive loss is beneficial in low-lable settings.

## 3.4.1 Method

As mentioned, current methods for image captioning typically adopt a single-view formulation, either by encoding the input image into only a single view or by concatenating multiple views into one single view. In Sec. 3.4.2, we derive a probabilistic model of image captioning and show that multi-view ensembling emerges naturally in the derivation. We compare these two formulations and point out the potential issues of the single-view formulation. In Sec. 3.4.3, we describe optimization challenges of multi-view ensembling and propose an approximation to make the problem tractable. We then propose a concrete implementation of multi-view ensembling with a transformer encoder-decoder architecture in Sec. 3.4.4. Lastly, in Sec. 3.4.5, in addition to the standard loss for word prediction, we propose for the views to be regarded as augmentations of the input image, and thus we introduce a contrastive loss \[83, 84\] to regularize the representation of the views.

## 3.4.5 Auxiliary Contrastive Loss

Since the output of the model remains the same, we can train with the standard cross entropy loss or the SCST loss for the generated words. We term this loss ℒword. Next, we propose to regard the views as _augmentations of the input image, which is enabled by the fact that they are encoded separately as_ described above. We therefore add a contrastive loss con across views to help the representation learning of the encoded heterogeneous views. Note that this is only possible if we encode the views separately and regard each view as an augmentation of the input image. Implementation-wise, to learn the representation of each view, a learnable \[CLS\] token is prepended to each view before sending into the transformer encoder. The encoded views from the same input image are positive pairs and the views from different images are negative pairs. To further augment the views, we also apply dropout along the channel, sequence, and view dimensions, with drop rate p _c_, p _s_, and p _v_, respectively. It has been shown by Gao et al. \[89\] and Liu et al. \[90\] that simple augmentation introduced by dropout is sufficient for learning a good sentence-level representation. For channel-wise dropout, each channel across views and sequences are randomly zero-ed out with probability p _c_. For sequence-wise dropout, each token, which is a d-dimensional feature vector, across views are randomly zero-ed out with probability p _s_. For view-wise dropout, each view, which is a matrix of shape S d where _S is the sequence length of a view, is randomly removed with probability pv_. The final loss is thus ℒ = ℒword + λℒcon.

## 3.4.6 Implementation Details

We integrate the proposed multi-view hierarchical ensembling into the ℳ 2 image captioning model \[74\]. For the contrastive loss, we adapt MoCo-v2 \[91\] with an exponential moving average (EMA) transformer encoder and a memory buffer of size 10000. The weight for contrastive loss λ _con_ is tuned and set to 0.05 for cross- entropy training and 0.2 for SCST training. The drop rates p _c_, p _s_, and p _v_ are all set to 0.1 following Gao et al. \[89\] without tuning. To generate views of the input image, we use (1) objects detected by Faster-RCNN pre-trained on Visual Genome \[1\], (2) flattened image grid features from CLIP ViT-B/32 pre-trained model \[63\], (3) whole, five-crops, and nine-crops cross-modal textual contexts (Txt-Ctx) retrieved by CLIP ViT-L/14 pre-trained model \[3\]. Note that all models for generating the views are frozen so that all views are pre-computed offline. For (1), by regarding views as augmentations, we naturally choose to use a _shared transformer_ encoder to encode each view independently. Compared to methods that concatenate all views into a long sequence as input \[77, 78, 3\], where the computational complexity scales up quadratically with respect to the number of views, our method scales up linearly. Compared to models that use entire models per view \[73, 74, 75, 76\] or methods that encode each view with unshared encoders \[93, 94, 95, 96\], our method is more parameter efficient. Furthermore, data augmentation increases data diversity and thus improves data efficiency, which is particularly important for training data-hungry transformer models. Last but not least, by regarding heterogeneous views generated by different pre-trained models as augmentations of the input image, we incorporate a contrastive loss in a novel way to help representation learning of heterogeneous views and increase data efficiency \[85, 87, 88\]. Different from how other VL methods \[63, 97, 98, 93, 99\] incorporate a contrastive loss, our formulation does not require annotated pairs (e.g. human annotated image-caption pairs in MS-COCO or image-text pairs scraped from the internet \[100\]) and can work with unlabeled image-only data to achieve better performance. Also crucially, for (2) we devise a hierarchical decoder layer, which modifies the standard transformer decoder layer by introducing two-tiered cross-attention modules. ## Implementation Details

Our proposed HAAV can be easily incorporated into existing transformer encoder-decoder IC models. In this paper, we choose the state-of-art Xmodal-Ctx \[3\] as our base model. Following the conventional training procedure \[74, 77, 102\], the model is first trained with cross-entropy loss and then fine-tuned with SCST \[75\] loss, which optimizes CIDEr score by reinforcement learning (note this is done by all compared methods). The dropout rates p _c_, p _s_, and p _t_ are all set to 0.1 following \[89\] without tuning. We reuse the heterogeneous views from previous methods without modifications, including detected objects from \[1\], CLIP ViT-B/32 \[63\] image grid features from \[2\], and text descriptions of image regions from \[3\]. For the contrastive loss, we prepend a learnable \[CLS\] token for each input view _v before sending it into the IC-encoder and use the encoded \[CLS\] token as a view-level representation_ for computing the contrastive loss. We use MoCo-v2 \[91\] with an exponential moving average (EMA) transformer encoder and a memory buffer to compute the contrastive loss. More implementation details and hyper-parameters can be found in the supplementary.

## 3.5 Semi-Supervised Object Detection through Cross-Match

In this section, we detail our methods for semi-supervised object detection, by leveraging a denser gradient signal from pseudolabels \[22\]. A great deal of work, including by our group, has been done on semi-supervised image classification. One popular line of research for SSL can be summarized as generating artificial labels on unlabeled images and feeding those unlabeled images with artificial labels through loss functions to train the models. For instance, pseudo-labelling \[103, 104, 105, 106\] (also known as self-training \[107, 108\]) produces labels generated from the model’s predictions themselves. Typically, confidence-based thresholding is used to filter out predictions that are low-confidence and hence likely to be incorrect. Consistency regularization \[109, 29, 28, 27, 110, 51\] applies different perturbations to inputs or models and enforces predictions under these perturbations to be consistent. The consistency constraint is usually applied through soft labels (i.e., distillation) though it is also possible to do it through hard labels \[51\] where predictions are converted intohard (one-hot) labels. Although great success has been achieved for SSL in the image classification context using these methods, translating these techniques to SSL for object detection has only recently begun to be explored \[7, 111, 112, 113, 114\]. In translating these techniques to object detection, the typical process used to generate pseudo-labels is extracting a dense set of bounding box predictions, followed by confidence thresholding and non-maximum suppression (NMS). However, a direct translation of pseudo-labeling does not fully consider the characteristics of the object detector training. For example, since hard decisions are made based on probability-based thresholding, only a small number of bounding boxes make it through this thresholding to eventually become pseudo-labels. Some of these pseudo-labels may still be incorrect and, more importantly, Region of Interests (RoIs) that are highly overlapped with false negatives (i.e., boxes with real objects that are filtered out) will be treated incorrectly as background or get ignored during the training process. As a result, the overall gradient signal produced by such pseudo-labeling is weak (i.e., there will only be a few positives, and several sources of error could result in degradation of the signal) and sparse (i.e., across the image andobjects). In this work, we present our method, CrossMatch, to address these problems by seeking to strengthen the gradient signal in two ways. First, we identify a key source of rich information already inherent in many object detection approaches:

**3.5.4 CrossMatch** To address the issue of sparse and weak gradient signal in pseudo-labeling methods (Figure 15), we introduce CrossMatch. The intuition behind our method is that we can propagate gradient signals through multiple paths from multi-scale methods. Specifically, our proposed method for semi-supervised object detection enforces consistency between different levels of the feature pyramid generated by the feature _pyramid network (FPN) \[115\]. See Figure 16 forillustration._ The FPN generates a set of multi-scale feature maps {P2\*, P3, P4, P5, P6\*} , which are used in both stages of two-stage detectors1. The region proposal network (RPN) uses these feature maps to produce multi-scale region of interests (RoIs). Once the RoIs are collected, two-stage detectors like Faster-RCNN \[116\] assigns only one particular level of features to each RoI determined by a heuristic function (Equation 26) based on spatial dimensions of RoIs (and ignores other levels): We argue that different levels of features on the feature pyramid can be viewed as feature representations at different scales and therefore propose a novel method to enforce consistency between different scales. The fact that this includes smaller scales, but potentially in a soft manner (see Section 3.5.6), would result in a denser (but still weak) signal that can be used for semi-supervised training. Specifically, the student network makes predictions using each level of {P2\*, P3, P4, P5\*} and the teacher network generates artificial labels using the features determined by the heuristic function. Although we can also use all scales for the teacher, the heuristic function ensures the appropriate scale is used to generate reliable artificial labels. We empirically found that using all scales for the teacher is computationally intensive and did not improve performance. The unsupervised loss function is computed by averaging the loss between each of student predictions and artificial labels, which is described in the next sections. Unlike prior work that applies the consistency constraint with either soft labels \[109, 29, 28, 27\] or hard labels \[51\], and in order to further densify the gradient signal, CrossMatch enforces consistency between different scales by using bothsoft and hard labels. We show in experiments that this is a crucial design for semi-supervised object detection especially with limited labeled data.

**3.5.6 Consistency with Soft Labels**

## Limitation with Hard Labels Even though hard labelling has achieved recent success in semi-supervised

object detection, there are still possible limitations to this approach. The standard object detection training process involves matching RoIs to labels. RoIs that are matched with labels (when the intersection-over-union score is above the threshold) are sampled as positive examples and the rest is treated as backgrounds (or ignored). However, due to confidence thresholding, it is possible that no (or inaccurate) psuedo-labels are generated in some object regions. Unlike semi-supervised image classification where the low-confident images are simply excluded from training, RoIs that are highly overlapped with those false-negative regions can be mistakenly treated as backgrounds which can be a potential source of erroraccumulation. To tackle this problem, we propose to combine soft labels with hard labels. For each unlabeled image, we first use the Teacher’s region proposal network (RPN) to produce a list of RoIs {R _i}i=1_ ^𝑁𝑁 where N is the total number of proposals. ## 3.6 Advancements in Active Learning

## 3.6.1 Summary

One of the ways to learn good models using less labels is by using active learning to select the most informative samples to acquire labels for. Based on some prior work in our group \[121, 122\], we developed a new method to select samples actively with the underlying goal of improving the embedding using information theoretic metrics. This method, being primarily dependent on the embeddings of the dataset, is agnostic to the task being considered. Hence our method, InfoNN is a unified framework for AL which can be used in any problem where a key component is learning the embedding of the dataset. We demonstrated the versatility of the proposed method by experimenting with both supervised classification and deep metric learning and exhibiting improved performance \[23\].

## 3.6.2 Introduction

A defining feature of modern machine learning is the reliance on large volumes of human-labeled data. Perhaps the most prominent example is the existence of massive hand-labelled image datasets, but the task of acquiring large amounts of human-provided data is nearly ubiquitous in machine learning. However, such data is not free; it is often tedious and expensive to gather a sufficient number of query responses to satisfy data hungry machine learning models. Active learning (AL) \[123\] seeks to mitigate this issue by carefully selecting only the most informative samples to be labelled. More generally, AL attempts to identify the most informative queries to pose to an oracle. These queries can include asking for a class label or rating, or more general relational queries such as the similarity (or dissimilarity) of different items. Classification relies on models (e.g., neural networks) with the ability to learn good representations of the data. Active classification focuses on how to best solicit labels for unlabelled data points, with many modern approaches either implicitly or explicitly relying on the representations learned to determine the most informative label. Methods that use metrics based on the predicted class probabilities, such as uncertainty \[124\] or consistency \[125\], implicitly rely on such representations, whereas core-set based approaches \[126, 127\] directly use learned representations to select diverse samples. Thus, if we seek the most informative labels with respect to improving the learned representation of our classification model, it enables our method to be task agnostic. Here, we present a unified framework, which is made feasible by a novel type of similarity query that can be applied to any problem which involves learning a representation of the data. Specifically, we consider the nearest neighbor (NN) query, which, given a reference data point r, asks an oracle (e.g., a human expert) to select the most similar point from among a set of C alternatives _t1, t2,..., tC_. We denote this a length C NN query. With the goal of minimizing the required number of queries, we adapt an active query selection strategy to this query type. We take an information theoretic approach and estimate the gain in mutual information (conditioned on previous query responses) as the criteria for selecting the most informative query, an approach that we dub Info-NN.

3.6.5 Unified framework for active classification and metric learning

This view of active classification gives rise to a unified framework which can be used in either active
classification or active Deep Metric Learning (DML): from a pool of candidate NN queries, choose the
most informative query to ask the oracle, then re-train the model to incorporate the newly acquired
query response. Despite each problem seemingly requiring fundamentally different oracle
responses (similarity information vs. labels), both problems can be tackled utilizing NN queries,
and thus, the same active query selection strategy. The main difference is the pool of candidate
queries. In active DML, we can query the oracle for similarity information about any set of items,
whereas in active classification, the pool of candidate NN queries is restricted to queries that contain one
item from every class. This pool of candidate queries is formed by setting every zi corresponding to an
xi ∈ U as the reference point, and finding (up to) C nearest neighbors of differing classes. A critical
feature of this unified framework is that it does not depend on which measure of “informativeness”
is used. This allows for a practitioner to plug-in their desired active query selection criteria
without making any modifications to the framework, as depicted in Fig. 17. In our experiments, we
select the queries that maximize mutual information for both active DML and classification experiments.

## 4.2 Manifold Transport Operators

## 4.2.1 CelebA Augmentations

We first show results in unsupervised learning of natural variations in a dataset using the manifold autoencoder (MAE) framework \[40, 18\]. To effectively train the MAE, we must select training point pairs that are close on the data manifold. We do this for each training point by selecting nearest neighbors in the intermediary layer of a ResNet18 classifier pretrained on ImageNet. This approach is known as perceptual similarity \[140\] and has successfully been applied for style transfer and image-to-image translation. We find that perceptual similarity is effective in denoting point pairs that result in semantically meaningful transformations without labels, as depicted in Figure 19. In this figure we also compare to other methods that learn unsupervised transformations using a similar network architecture. The β-VAE \[141\] encourages disentanglement of latent dimensions by reweighting the KL-divergence term in the VAE objective. We note how this model learns similar transformations as the MAE, at the cost of sacrificing reconstruction quality. Additionally, the contractive autoencoder (CAE) \[142\] paths coincide with directions of motion on a linear tangent plane at each latent vector. ## 4.3.1 Model architecture details

CLIP \[63\] has two encoders, CLIP-Image and CLIP-Text which are pre-trained transformer models for image and text. CLIP-Text is a base transformer model consisting of 12 layers, a hidden size of 768, and the final linear projection layer produces a representation vector of size 512. CLIP-Image is a hybrid ViT-Base model (which is the same as the DINO-trained model used for fair comparison) consisting of 12 stacked layers, with a convolutional layer in the beginning for feature extraction. For a given image, a total of 49 embedding vectors with a hidden size of 768 are generated, and to match the output of the CLIP-Text encoder; the output hidden state is projected from 768 to 512 dimensions. We fine-tune the last block of the vision transformer starting with a learning rate of 5e-5 decaying it over time using a cosine annealed schedule. We train the model for 100 epochs using batches of size 128 and set the value of λ to

0.25 in the loss function above. Tuning andtesting is done on a separate validation set to select the best hyperparameters.

## 4.6.1 Info-NN applied to metriclearning

As an example, we applied the Info-NN framework to active metric learning. Learning an embedding or representation of the data that accurately reflects similarity between items is the goal of metric learning. We directly query an oracle for perceptual similarity information, as is done in \[169\], where triplets of the form “Is item B or item C more similar to item A?” are actively selected for learning an embedding of items. Active deep metric learning (DML) builds on this idea by finding the most informative queries to ask the oracle. We conducted experiments on a food dataset consists of 72, 148 crowdsourced triplets gathered for 73 different food items \[170\]. We utilize a neural network to learn an embedding that matches the oracle’s responses to similarity queries. Because a length C NN query can be decomposed into C 1 triplets, we utilize a triplet loss \[171\]. To measure the performance of our embedding learning algorithm, we use triplet generalization accuracy, which records the fraction of test triplets whose ordering is consistent with the learned embedding. A sample result is illustrated in Fig. 24.

# 5.0 Conclusions

Across this program, we have developed a range of methods tackling zero-shot, semi-supervised, and low-labeled image classification, image captioning, and object detection. Our methods have been strongly cited and influenced the field, while at the same time producing real-world impact through artifacts such as open-source code. Specifically, we developed the following methods:

1. **Leveraging the Manifold-Structure through FeatMatch \[13\]**\- Novel methods for graph (manifold)-based augmentation for semi-supervised image classification.
2. **Leveraging the Manifold-Structure through Transport Operators \[14, 15, 16, 17, 18\] - A** series of methods for learning manifold transport operators in an efficient manner on real-world data, integrated within semi-supervised learning pipelines to improve performance.
3. **Semi-Supervised Clustering and Retrieval for Zero-Shot Learning \[19\] - Novel methods for** integrating semi- supervised clustering and retrieval, within large-scale pre-trained feature spaces, to perform effective zero-shot learn- ing.
4. **Low-Labeled Captioning through Retrieval \[20, 21\]**-Methods for retrieval-based augmentation of images, which can be seen as additional views of the data, and efficient and effective architectures for exploiting them for low-labeled image captioning.
5. **Semi-Supervised Object Detection through Cross-Match \[22\] - Methods for improving** gradient flow in existing semi-supervised object detection methods to significantly improve performance.
6. **Advancements in Active Learning \[23\] - Unified view of active learning with connections to** deep metric learning, and a novel method Info-NN for selecting queries using information-theoretic criterion. During this time, other advancements have also changed the field. Specifically, large-scale pre-trained models (i.e. Foundation Models) have recently shown that the range of methods we have utilized (combinations of self-supervised/contrastive learning, clustering, pseudo-labeling, and data selection) can be scaled up to produce emergent properties including strong performance and robustness to out-of- distribution data. Such advancements have generated a great deal of excitement, and indeed pose significant new opportunities to even further push the envelope on low-labeled learning.

Under the special condition that the observed targets are straight ahead and moving nearly in the same direction as the observing vehicle, like in adaptive cruise control (ACC) systems, those models work well. In more general scenarios, where movements of other vehicles have to be tracked in all possible directions and all around the vehicle (e.g. in inner-city or intersection situations), the modeling is insufficient. This paper aims at tracking vehicles from monocular intensity image sequences and presents an efficient and robust approach to three-dimensional (3-D) model-based vehicle tracking. Under the weak perspective assumption and the ground-plane constraint, the movements of model projection in the two-dimensional image plane can be decomposed into two motions: translation and rotation. They are the results of the corresponding movements of 3-D translation on the ground plane (GP) and rotation around the normal of the GP, which can be determined separately. A new metric based on point-to-line segment distance is proposed to evaluate the similarity between an image region and an instantiation of a 3-D vehicle model under a given pose. Based on this, we provide an efficient pose refinement method to refine the vehicle's pose parameters. An improved EKF is also proposed to track and to predict vehicle motion with a precise kinematics model. Experimental results with both indoor and outdoor data show that the algorithm obtains desirable performance even under severe occlusion and clutter.

## Abstract

### Background:

Remote patient monitoring (RPM) programs augment type 1 diabetes (T1D) care based on retrospective continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) data. Few methods are available to estimate the likelihood of a patient experiencing clinically significant hypoglycemia within one week.

### Methods:

We developed a machine learning model to estimate the probability that a patient will experience a clinically significant hypoglycemic event, defined as CGM readings below 54 mg/dL for at least 15 consecutive minutes, within one week. The model takes as input the patient’s CGM time series over a given week, and outputs the predicted probability of a clinically significant hypoglycemic event the following week. We used 10-fold cross-validation and external validation (testing on cohorts different from the training cohort) to evaluate performance. We used CGM data from three different cohorts of patients with T1D: REPLACE-BG (226 patients), Juvenile Diabetes Research Foundation (JDRF; 355 patients) and Tidepool (120 patients).

### Results:

In 10-fold cross-validation, the average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC-AUC) was 0.77 (standard deviation \[SD\]: 0.0233) on the REPLACE-BG cohort, 0.74 (SD: 0.0188) on the JDRF cohort, and 0.76 (SD: 0.02) on the Tidepool cohort. In external validation, the average ROC-AUC across the three cohorts was 0.74 (SD: 0.0262).

### Conclusions:

We developed a machine learning algorithm to estimate the probability of a clinically significant hypoglycemic event within one week. Predictive algorithms may provide diabetes care providers using RPM with additional context when prioritizing T1D patients for review.

**Keywords:** hypoglycemia prediction, continuous glucose monitoring, type 1 diabetes, clinical decision support, patient prioritization, machine learning

## Introduction

Artificial intelligence–based prioritization algorithms for type 1 diabetes (T1D) patients based on continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) data have been shown to improve patients’ glucose control and to increase clinic capacity and efficiency.[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr1-19322968241236208)-[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr3-19322968241236208) Existing patient prioritization algorithms are based on consensus glucose targets[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr4-19322968241236208) calculated on the most recent two weeks of CGM data. Among the key consensus glucose metrics[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr4-19322968241236208) are time below 54 mg/dL (clinically significant hypoglycemia), between 54 and 70 mg/dL (hypoglycemia), between 70 and 180 mg/dL (target range), between 180 and 250 mg/dL (hyperglycemia), and above 250 mg/dL (clinically significant hyperglycemia). Whereas hyperglycemia increases the risk of long-term complications, clinically significant hypoglycemia increases the risk of severe hypoglycemia, which requires immediate attention and can be life-threatening. Remote patient monitoring (RPM) offers the opportunity to review CGM data and titrate insulin doses more frequently, and may help minimize the risk of clinically significant hypoglycemia.

Prioritization algorithms for T1D patients could benefit from a forward-looking indicator of hypoglycemic risk, such as an estimate of the likelihood that the patient will experience a hypoglycemic event in the near future. Numerous machine learning models have been proposed for predicting hypoglycemic events from CGM data. Models include logistic regression,[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr5-19322968241236208), [6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr6-19322968241236208) support vector machines,[7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr7-19322968241236208), [8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr8-19322968241236208) random forests,[5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr5-19322968241236208), [8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr8-19322968241236208) gradient-boosted trees[6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr6-19322968241236208), [9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr9-19322968241236208) and neural networks.[8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr8-19322968241236208)-[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr12-19322968241236208) See Zhang et al[13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr13-19322968241236208) for a detailed review and discussion. Most models have been developed with the aim of incorporating the predictions in a real-time system (such as a smartphone application) that would anticipate the hypoglycemic event and prompt the patient to intervene. As a result, most models consider short prediction horizons between 15 and 60 minutes.

The current literature offers few tools to predict hypoglycemic events one week in advance, a time frame relevant for many RPM programs. To the best of our knowledge, only one article has been published on predicting the weekly risk of hypoglycemia in T1D patients using CGM data.[14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr14-19322968241236208) The authors used a gradient-boosting classifier trained on a set of 26 predefined features computed on one week of CGM measurements, such as the mean glucose and the coefficient of variation, to predict the risk of excessive hypoglycemia over the following week. The authors used two different definitions of excessive hypoglycemia: time below 70 mg/dL greater than 4% and time below 70 mg/dL greater than its historical 90th percentile.

## Methods

### Overview

We developed a machine learning algorithm that uses a week of CGM data to predict the probability that the patient will experience a clinically significant hypoglycemic event over the subsequent week. We define a clinically significant hypoglycemic event as the patient’s glucose level remaining below 54 mg/dL for at least 15 consecutive minutes, in line with consensus guidance.[4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr4-19322968241236208)

### Data

We develop and validate the machine learning algorithm using three data sets:

- REPLACE-BG: The source of the data is the REPLACE-BG clinical trial ( [NCT02258373](https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02258373)). The data were obtained from the Jaeb Center for Health Research (JCHR) Web site.[15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr15-19322968241236208) The aim of the study was to determine the efficacy and safety of making insulin dosing decisions based on CGM alone without confirmatory blood glucose monitoring (BGM) in adults with T1D. The study lasted for 26 weeks and included 226 participants. The CGM data were recorded using a Dexcom G4 Platinum CGM System. The study was completed in 2016 and the results are discussed in Aleppo et al.[16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr16-19322968241236208)

- Juvenile Diabetes Research Foundation (JDRF): The source of the data is the JDRF CGM RCT clinical trial ( [NCT00406133](https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT00406133)). The data were obtained from the JCHR Web site.[17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr17-19322968241236208) The aim of the study was to determine whether the use of CGM as a supplement to BGM can improve glycemic control and quality of life in children and adults with T1D. The study lasted for 12 months and included 451 participants. The CGM data were recorded using Medtronic Guardian, Dexcom STS, and Abbott Diabetes FreeStyle Navigator sensors. The study was completed in 2009 and the results are discussed in JDRF CGM Study Group.[18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr18-19322968241236208)

- Tidepool: The data set was donated to us by Tidepool, Palo Alto, California ( [https://www.tidepool.org/](https://www.tidepool.org/)). It contains the CGM time series of 120 patients between July 25, 2015 and August 7, 2018. The CGM data were recorded with different types of sensors: Freestyle Navigator, Dexcom STS, Medtronic Paradigm or Guardian, iPro2, iPro2 Professional CGM, Freestyle Libre Pro Flash, and Dexcom G4.


### Machine Learning Algorithm

The CGM time series are split into nonoverlapping sequences each spanning one week. The one-week sequences have varying length, depending on for how long the CGM device was worn by the patient during the week. We include sequences that have at least 70% of the maximum possible number of readings, in line with consensus guidance (Danne, Nimri and Battelino, 2017).

The machine learning model is trained on pairs of consecutive one-week sequences. The input to the model is based on the first week represented by a sequence of CGM readings (eg, 2016 readings for a patient wearing a five-minute CGM sensor 100% of the time) and the output is based on the second week represented by a binary label, which is 1 if the patient experienced a clinically significant hypoglycemic event during this week (positive class), and 0 otherwise (negative class). One model is trained for each cohort of patients; the input sequences and output labels are pooled together across all patients in the cohort.

The input sequences are transformed using the Minimally Random Convolutional Kernel Transform (MiniRocket).[19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr19-19322968241236208) We use the MiniRocket code as provided by the authors with no changes.[20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr20-19322968241236208) We use the experimental version of the code, which supports variable length inputs, given that the input sequences of different patients have different lengths as the patients do not always wear the CGM device. The MiniRocket algorithm transforms each input sequence into a fixed-length embedding vector by performing a large number of convolutions. The length of the embedding vector, which is approximately 10 000, does not depend on the length of the input sequence.

The embedding vectors are then used together with the class labels for training a classifier. We use an L1 and L2 regularized linear classifier trained with gradient descent, which we implement in TensorFlow. We set the L1 penalty to 0.005 and the L2 penalty to 0.05. We train the model with a learning rate 0.00001 and a batch size of 32 for a minimum of 100 epochs and a maximum of 1000 epochs using early stopping. To determine when to stop training, we set aside 30% of the training set as validation set. If the validation loss has not decreased over the previous 10 epochs, then we stop training and restore the best parameters, that is, the parameters (weights and biases) corresponding to the smallest validation loss.

The class probabilities predicted by the linear classifier are compared with a decision threshold to obtain the predicted class labels. If the predicted probability is greater than the threshold, we predict a positive label (i.e., 1), otherwise we predict a negative label (i.e., 0). To select the decision threshold, we consider values between 0.01 and 0.99 with a step size of 0.01 and we choose the one that minimizes the difference between sensitivity and specificity on the training data.

We make our code available open source.[21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr21-19322968241236208)

We validate the machine learning algorithm using two different techniques:

- _Ten-fold cross-validation_: The CMG sequences are randomly split into 10 subsamples of equal size (folds), with each subsample containing approximately the same fraction of positively labeled sequences (ie, the splits are stratified). Out of the 10 subsamples, nine subsamples are combined and used as training data, whereas one subsample is used as test data. This process is repeated 10 times, with each of the 10 subsamples used exactly once as test data. We perform 10-fold cross-validation separately for each cohort.

- _External validation_: We train the model on a given cohort, and then evaluate the pretrained model both on the same cohort (training cohort) and on all the other cohorts (test cohorts).


We additionally conduct the following robustness checks:

- _Sensitivity to time-to-first-event_: To assess the ability of the model to predict clinically significant hypoglycemic events at different future time horizons, we study the sensitivity of the percentage of true positives to the time-to-first-event, defined as the time until the first clinically significant hypoglycemic event occurs during the week for which we generate the predictions.

- _Sensitivity to hyperparameters_: To assess the robustness of the model to the hyperparameters, we rerun the 10-fold cross-validation analysis using different values of the learning rate, batch size, and L1 and L2 regularization penalties. We do not study the sensitivity to the number of training epochs, given that this is not a fixed hyperparameter but is instead selected during training using early stopping. Given that performing a comprehensive grid search is computationally prohibitive, we limit the hyperparameter grid to 36 plausible combinations.


## Results

### Data Quality

We exclude the CGM time series recorded by the Abbott Diabetes sensors from the JDRF data set, given that, differently from all other CGM time series, they have a frequency of 10 minutes instead of five minutes. As a result, the JDRF cohort used for the analysis includes 355 of the initial 451 participants. We also drop all CGM readings outside the range of the device that are lower than 40 mg/dL or greater than 400 mg/dL, from all three data sets. Apart from the above, no additional preprocessing or transformations are applied to the data prior to training the machine learning algorithm.

The mean glucose is 160 mg/dL, with a standard deviation (SD) of 63 mg/dL ( [Table 1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#table1-19322968241236208)), resulting in a coefficient of variation of 39%. #### Sensitivity to time-to-first-event

The results indicate that, although the model can detect clinically significant hypoglycemic events at all considered future time horizons, the percentage of positive classifications decreases as the time distance to the event increases. The average percentage of true positives across the three cohorts decreases from 79% for events taking place within 1 day to 55% for events taking place after 6 days ( [Figures 4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#fig4-19322968241236208)- [6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#fig6-19322968241236208)).

The results indicate that the model is robust to the hyperparameters ( [Figure 7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#fig7-19322968241236208)). The average ROC-AUC across the three cohorts over the 36 considered hyperparameter combinations is 0.77 (SD: 0.0793) on the training set and 0.71 on the test set (SD: 0.0412). ## Discussion

Using retrospective data from three independent cohorts, we developed a machine learning model that uses one week of CGM data to estimate the risk of a clinically significant hypoglycemic event in the following week. This fills a gap in the current literature, where the focus is almost exclusively on the problem of predicting hypoglycemic events from CGM data over short time horizons such as 30 and 60 minutes, as used in automated insulin delivery systems. The ability to estimate the risk of hypoglycemia a week in advance may benefit patient prioritization for prospective glucose management currently deployed in a variety of centers.[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr22-19322968241236208)- [24](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr24-19322968241236208)

These results indicate that the model has a fair ability to predict whether a patient will experience a clinically significant hypoglycemic event within one week. The average ROC-AUC in 10-fold cross-validation is 0.81 on the training set and 0.76 on the test set. The average ROC-AUC in external validation is 0.8 on the training set and 0.74 on the test set. The difference between the model performance metrics on the training and test sets is not substantial, which indicates that the model does not overfit.

However, the model extrapolates better to new unseen data from the same cohort that were used for training than to data from different external cohorts. This indicates that, in practice, the model should be trained on the same cohort on which it is planned to be used for inference.

Furthermore, although our model can successfully predict clinically significant hypoglycemic events at all considered future time horizons, the number of positive classifications decreases as the time distance to the event increases. The results suggest that, in practice, a positive prediction is more likely to indicate an event taking place within 3 to 4 days than in 4 to 7 days.

The main limitation of our model is that it is not interpretable and, being a pure time series model (similar to),[12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr12-19322968241236208) explanation techniques, such as feature importance and attribution, are not available. Although our model can predict whether a patient will experience a clinically significant hypoglycemic event over the subsequent week with some level of accuracy, the model does not provide any information about which specific characteristics of the most recent patient’s CGM readings (such as increased glycemic variability) have led to make this prediction.

An additional limitation of our analysis is that the data were recorded with early stage CGM devices that may not have been as accurate as the ones currently available. Furthermore, our analysis uses directly the raw data provided by the CGM sensors and no preprocessing is applied to account for potential miscalibrations, sensor signal dropouts, or pressure-induced sensor attenuation (PISA) effects.[25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr25-19322968241236208) Data from newer sensors with the ability to filter out PISA effects could improve the predictive ability of our model.

Future research should investigate whether the accuracy of the model can be improved by training the model on sub-cohorts of patients defined by type of therapy (multiple daily injections vs insulin pump). The inclusion of additional inputs from different sensors, such as insulin pumps, heart rate monitors, and activity trackers,[26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr26-19322968241236208), [27](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr27-19322968241236208) could also improve model performance. Further work could also investigate incorporating patient socioeconomic, demographic, or behavioral characteristics. In addition, the model should be reevaluated on more recent data from patients, using newer CGM sensors in combination with automated insulin delivery systems. Although automated insulin delivery systems greatly reduce clinically significant hypoglycemia, forward-looking algorithms could augment safety and help physicians provide guidance on glucose management.

We are investigating how to best integrate the model in tools currently deployed in clinical practice, such as Timely Interventions for Diabetes Excellence (TIDE), an open-source tool for personalized T1D care based on CGM data at the population scale.[1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr1-19322968241236208)-[3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11572183/#bibr3-19322968241236208) The addition of this feature would be TIDE’s first predictive component.

## Conclusion

We developed a machine learning algorithm for estimating a prospective indicator of clinically significant hypoglycemia in patients with T1D within one week. The new indicator could be used by diabetes care providers in combination with standard consensus glucose targets when prioritizing patients for review or to inform guidance on glucose management.
